title: Diffusion Removes Langevin’s Conditioning Dependence: A Sharp Gaussian Analysis

paper.title: Diffusion Removes Langevin’s Conditioning Dependence: A Sharp Gaussian Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Despite their empirical success, why diffusion models overcome the bottlenecks of classical score-based samplers remains unclear. In this work, we leverage Gaussian distributions to isolate this phenomenon. We establish 2-Wasserstein convergence bounds for optimized hyperparameters, showing that diffusion processes achieve a sampling error of O ⁡ ( d ​ λ max ​ log ⁡ N / N ) O(\sqrt{d\lambda_{\max}}\log N/N) , where d d is the dimension, N N the number of sampling steps, and λ max \lambda_{\max} the largest eigenvalue of the target covariance matrix. Unadjusted and underdamped Langevin dynamics suffer from an additional κ \sqrt{\kappa} factor, where κ \kappa is the condition number. These rates follow from spectral bounds which are sharp: we confirm them via matching first-order asymptotics as N → ∞ N\rightarrow\infty . Our analysis provides a rigorous characterization, in the Gaussian setting, of how time-dependent score trajectories remove condition-number dependence during sampling. By contrast, in the learning phase, we show that estimating the unnoised score by gradient descent leads to essentially the same estimator as estimating a noisy score, which suggests that the benefits of noising do not come from the learning phase.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Since their introduction, diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of domains ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Kong et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . Training diffusion models requires estimating the gradient of the log-density (the so-called score ) of a noisy version of the target. Then samples are produced by iterative denoising through a formula involving this score. Taking a step back, iterative score-based sampling strategies long predate modern diffusion models, as epitomized by the celebrated Langevin algorithm ( Pavliotis, 2014 ; Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 ) and its many variants such as underdamped Langevin ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2015 ) . The key factors explaining their success compared to those more classical algorithms are still unclear: what exact role does the noising process in diffusion models play, and how does it interact with the learning and sampling phases? Our primary goal in this work is to prove a separation in sampling efficiency between diffusion models and Langevin dynamics in terms of their dependence on the condition number. This sheds light on the practical effectiveness of diffusion models on ill-conditioned distributions such as natural images ( Guth et al., 2022 ; Field, 1987 ) . To do so, we consider the class of (centered) Gaussian targets. Naturally, sampling from a Gaussian distribution is not our primary concern here. Rather, we use this analytically tractable setting to derive sharp convergence rates accompanied by matching asymptotics, in order to highlight how diffusion models overcome limitations of other score-based sampling methods. As discussed below, deriving tight condition-number dependence for more general target classes such as log-concave distributions is a long-standing open problem ( Cheng et al., 2018 ; Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, 2020 ) , which is outside the scope of the present paper. Additionally, we focus for most of the paper on the sampling phase, comparing the sampling convergence rates of diffusion, unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and underdamped Langevin dynamics (ULD). Assuming access to the true score yields a clean analysis and the separation between diffusion and Langevin, hence for simplicity we focus on this case. The connection with the estimation of the score in the learning phase is discussed in the latter part of our work.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: We establish upper bounds on the 2-Wasserstein error between the target distribution and the distribution sampled from the diffusion, ULA and ULD. Convergence rates are derived in Section 2 by optimizing these bounds with respect to hyperparameters (see Table 1 for summary). The bounds for diffusion and for Langevin differ by a factor proportional to the square root of the condition number. Thanks to explicit computations of the Wasserstein errors, we confirm these rates via matching first-order asymptotics. By contrast, in the learning phase, we show in Section 3 that estimating the unnoised score by gradient descent leads to essentially the same estimator as estimating a noisy score, the two differing only in how they regularize the directions unseen in the data, which suggests that the benefits of noising do not come from the learning phase. sections.heading: Related work.
sections.text: For ULA, a similar analysis of the two error terms was already performed, for example, by Durmus et al. (2019) ; Wibisono (2018) and specifically in the Gaussian case by Pedregosa (2023) . Building upon these works, we perform hyperparameter optimization and compute the asymptotic equivalent (rather than upper bounds). Many works have studied ULD in the log-concave case, see, e.g. , Cheng et al. (2018) ; Dalalyan and Riou-Durand (2020) ; Leimkuhler et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2026) for studies of the stochastic Euler scheme and Euler–Maruyama (EM) integrators. This line of work yields loose dependence on the condition number due to the bias term induced by non-vanishing step-sizes (see, e.g. , Eq. (11) in Dalalyan and Riou-Durand (2020) with a κ 3 / 2 \kappa^{3/2} in the complexity bound compared to our κ \sqrt{\kappa} ). A line of work has proved improved condition dependence for Gaussian targets ( Shen and Lee, 2019 ; Apers et al., 2024 ; Gouraud et al., 2025 ) , albeit with more complex integrators (splitting, random step-sizes, or Metropolis corrections). To our knowledge, the tight study of the bias of ULD for a Gaussian target and the EM integrator is a novel contribution. For diffusion models, Pierret and Galerne (2025) derive and numerically analyze error terms for Gaussian targets, but do not analytically derive optimal hyperparameters, discuss the dependence on the condition number, nor derive asymptotic equivalents. Closer are the works by Hurault et al. (2025) and Hurault et al. (2026) , which derive Wasserstein bounds for Gaussian data and discuss optimal hyperparameter choices depending on the covariance spectrum. A key difference with our work is that their analysis holds asymptotically for small step-sizes, whereas we make a fully non-asymptotic analysis (albeit in less generality), which enables us to capture the interaction between the step-size and other parameters, and to derive optimal step complexity with respect to our bounds. Wasserstein bounds beyond the Gaussian case are given for instance by Strasman et al. (2025) ; Beyler and Bach (2025) .

sections.heading: 2.1 Problem setup
sections.text: We denote by ℙ \mathbb{P} the target d d -dimensional centered Gaussian distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Σ ) \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) . Let ( λ i ) 1 ≤ i ≤ d (\lambda_{i})_{1\leq i\leq d} denote the eigenvalues of the positive-definite covariance matrix Σ \Sigma , and λ min \lambda_{\min} and λ max \lambda_{\max} be respectively the smallest and largest eigenvalues. The ratio κ := λ max λ min \kappa:=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} is the condition number of Σ \Sigma , which measures the degree of anisotropy of ℙ \mathbb{P} . Ill-conditioning is a classical source of difficulty for Langevin-based sampling methods, as their convergence rates typically deteriorate with κ \kappa ( Cheng et al., 2018 ; Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, 2020 ) . Let p p denote the Lebesgue density of ℙ \mathbb{P} . We define the score s s of the target distribution as s : x ↦ ∇ log ⁡ p ​ ( x ) = − Σ − 1 ​ x . s:x\mapsto\nabla\log p(x)=-\Sigma^{-1}x. We assume that the score is known exactly in this section; the learning problem is studied separately in Section 3 . We measure sampling error in the 2-Wasserstein distance, denoted by W 2 W_{2} . For two centered Gaussians whose covariance matrices Σ 1 \Sigma_{1} and Σ 2 \Sigma_{2} commute, the distance reduces to the Fréchet distance ∥ Σ 1 1 / 2 − Σ 2 1 / 2 ∥ F \lVert\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}-\Sigma_{2}^{1/2}\rVert_{F} , with ∥ ⋅ ∥ F \lVert\cdot\rVert_{F} the Frobenius norm ( Gelbrich, 1990 ) . For each sampling scheme, we denote by ℙ k \mathbb{P}_{k} the law of its k k -th iterate.

sections.heading: Time-homogeneous Langevin samplers.
sections.text: We first consider the Langevin process associated with ℙ \mathbb{P} , d ​ X t = s ⁡ ( X t ) ​ d ​ t + 2 ​ d ​ W t , t ∈ ℝ + , X 0 = 0 , \,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=s(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\,t\in\mathbb{R}_{+},\,X_{0}=0, (1) where ( W t ) (W_{t}) is a standard Brownian motion. The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) ( Dalalyan, 2017 ) is simply the Euler–Maruyama discretization of the SDE in ( 1 ). Given a step-size η \eta , an iteration budget N N , and a sequence ( ξ k ) (\xi_{k}) of independent standard Gaussian vectors in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , it is defined by { X 0 = 0 , ∀ k ∈ { 0 , … , N − 1 } , X k + 1 = X k + η s ( X k ) + 2 ​ η ξ k . \begin{cases}X_{0}=0,\\ \forall k\in\{0,\dots,N-1\},\,X_{k+1}=X_{k}+\eta s(X_{k})+\sqrt{2\eta}\xi_{k}.\end{cases} (2) We next consider underdamped Langevin dynamics (ULD) ( Cheng et al., 2018 ) , which introduces an auxiliary velocity variable into the Langevin dynamics with the aim of accelerating convergence: { d ​ X t = V t ​ d ​ t , d ​ V t = − γ ​ V t ​ d ​ t + s ⁡ ( X t ) ​ d ​ t + 2 ​ γ ​ d ​ W t , ​ t ∈ ℝ + , \begin{cases}\,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=V_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t,\\ \,\mathrm{d}V_{t}=-\gamma V_{t}\,\mathrm{d}t+s(X_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\end{cases}t\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, (3) with initialization X 0 = V 0 = 0 X_{0}=V_{0}=0 , where γ > 0 \gamma>0 is the friction coefficient. We discretize these dynamics using the Euler–Maruyama scheme, yielding with the same notation as above { X k + 1 = X k + η ​ V k , V k + 1 = ( 1 − η ​ γ ) ​ V k + η ​ s ​ ( X k ) + 2 ​ η ​ γ ​ ξ k . \begin{cases}X_{k+1}=X_{k}+\eta V_{k},\\ V_{k+1}=(1-\eta\gamma)V_{k}+\eta s(X_{k})+\sqrt{2\eta\gamma}\xi_{k}.\end{cases} (4)

sections.heading: Time-inhomogeneous diffusion sampler.
sections.text: Diffusion-based sampling follows a different principle ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song et al., 2021 ) : rather than sampling directly with the score of the target distribution, it constructs a family of perturbed distributions and uses a time-dependent score along this family. Many conventions exist; we study the following one because it leads to telescoping cancellations in the computations, greatly simplifying our analysis (see Appendix C.2.1 ). Concretely, for a general (centered) target ℚ \mathbb{Q} , consider the forward noising process { d X t = d W t , t ∈ [ 0 , T ] , X 0 = X ∼ ℚ , \begin{cases}\,\mathrm{d}X_{t}=\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\,t\in[0,T],\\ X_{0}=X\sim\mathbb{Q},\end{cases} whose marginal ℚ t \mathbb{Q}_{t} at time t t has Lebesgue density q t q_{t} and score s t := ∇ log ⁡ q t s_{t}:=\nabla\log q_{t} . The forward diffusion gradually smooths the target distribution, and T T is chosen large enough so that ℚ T ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , T ​ I ) \mathbb{Q}_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0,T\operatorname{I}) , a distribution that is straightforward to sample from. Sampling proceeds by reversing this transformation, i.e. , by simulating the reverse-time SDE ( Anderson, 1982 ) { d Y t = s T − t ( Y t ) d t + d W t , t ∈ [ 0 , T − δ ] , Y 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , T ​ I ) , \begin{cases}\,\mathrm{d}Y_{t}=s_{T-t}(Y_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t+\,\mathrm{d}W_{t},\,t\in[0,T-\delta],\\ Y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,T\operatorname{I}),\end{cases} (5) where 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , T ​ I ) \mathcal{N}(0,T\operatorname{I}) replaces the intractable true marginal ℚ T \mathbb{Q}_{T} and δ > 0 \delta>0 is an early-stopping threshold, standard in the analysis of diffusion models, where it prevents a possible blow-up of the score as t → 0 t\to 0 ( De Bortoli, 2022 ; Benton et al., 2024 ) . In our Gaussian setting ℚ = ℙ \mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{P} , all these quantities are explicit: the marginal at time t t is ℚ t = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , C t ) \mathbb{Q}_{t}=\mathcal{N}(0,C_{t}) with C t = Σ + t ​ I C_{t}=\Sigma+t\operatorname{I} , and s t : x ↦ − C t − 1 ​ x , s_{t}:x\mapsto-C_{t}^{-1}x, whose Lipschitz constant ( λ min + t ) − 1 (\lambda_{\min}+t)^{-1} is bounded by ( λ min + δ ) − 1 (\lambda_{\min}+\delta)^{-1} on [ δ , T ] [\delta,T] . Since information about the target is concentrated near t = T − δ t=T-\delta , we discretize ( 5 ) using a decreasing sequence of step-sizes ( η k ) (\eta_{k}) instead of a constant η \eta . We fix a decreasing grid T = τ 0 > τ 1 > ⋯ > τ N = δ T=\tau_{0}>\tau_{1}>\cdots>\tau_{N}=\delta defining τ k = τ k − 1 − η k \tau_{k}=\tau_{k-1}-\eta_{k} for k ∈ { 1 , … , N } k\in\{1,\dots,N\} . The diffusion algorithm we study is then { Y 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , T ​ I ) , ∀ k = 1 , … , N , Y k = Y k − 1 + η k ​ s τ k − 1 ​ ( Y k − 1 ) + η k ​ ξ k . \begin{cases}Y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,T\operatorname{I}),\\ \forall k=1,\dots,N,\,\,Y_{k}=Y_{k-1}+\eta_{k}s_{\tau_{k-1}}(Y_{k-1})+\sqrt{\eta_{k}}\xi_{k}.\end{cases} (6) The main difference between diffusion and Langevin lies in the use of a time-dependent score s t s_{t} in the former. Langevin methods only use the target score s s , and therefore operate under a fixed geometry governed by κ \kappa . This leads, as we will show in Theorem 1 , to a penalizing κ \sqrt{\kappa} factor in the convergence rate. In contrast, diffusion progressively modifies the geometry of the score along the sampling trajectory. Indeed, note that the condition number associated with s t s_{t} is κ t = t + λ max t + λ min ​ ⟶ t → ∞ ​ 1 , \kappa_{t}=\frac{t+\lambda_{\max}}{t+\lambda_{\min}}\underset{t\rightarrow\infty}{\longrightarrow}1, decreasing from κ 0 = κ \kappa_{0}=\kappa to 1. Sampling therefore begins in a near-isotropic regime, and only gradually recovers the original conditioning of the target as the trajectory approaches t = 0 t=0 . This intuition is formalized in Theorem 3 , showing that the sampling complexity of diffusion is indeed independent of κ \kappa .

sections.heading: 2.3 Diffusion models: circumventing the condition-number dependence
sections.text: In contrast, diffusion models follow the scores s t s_{t} , whose conditioning κ t \kappa_{t} tends to 1 at large times, and achieve rates that depend on neither κ \kappa nor λ min \lambda_{\min} . The previous theorem gives a spectrum-adaptive bound. The simplified O ⁡ ( Tr ⁡ Σ ​ log ⁡ N / N ) O(\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma}\log N/N) rate is obtained when d d grows at most polynomially with N N . The following proposition shows that this growth assumption can be removed at the price of a coarser dependence on the spectrum. Proposition 4 . sections.heading: 3 Learning: the impact of noise on the implicit bias
sections.text: The previous results assume the score of the target distribution—or, for diffusion, its noisy versions s t s_{t} —to be known exactly. In practice, these scores must first be learned from (noisy) samples. The goal of this section is to study whether the noise introduced in diffusion models leads to a different score estimator. We are given a dataset 𝒟 = { x i } 1 ≤ i ≤ m \mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq m} of m m independent realizations of ℙ \mathbb{P} and denote by Σ ^ = 1 m ​ ∑ i = 1 m x i ​ x i ⊤ \hat{\Sigma}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top} the empirical covariance matrix. Since the score of a Gaussian distribution is linear, we consider the score model s A : x ↦ − A ​ x , s_{A}:x\mapsto-Ax, where A ∈ ℝ d × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} , which recovers the true score s s when A = Σ − 1 A=\Sigma^{-1} . When Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} is invertible, which is almost surely the case if m ≥ d m\geq d , the score-matching loss ( Hyvärinen, 2005 ) L : A ↦ 1 m ​ ∑ i = 1 m ( ∇ ⋅ s A ​ ( x i ) + 1 2 ​ ∥ s A ​ ( x i ) ∥ 2 ) , L:A\mapsto\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Big(\nabla\cdot s_{A}(x_{i})+\frac{1}{2}\lVert s_{A}(x_{i})\rVert^{2}\Big), (8) where ∥ ⋅ ∥ \lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the Euclidean norm, admits the unique minimizer Σ ^ − 1 \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} . In the overparameterized regime m < d m<d , however, it has no minimizer as it diverges towards − ∞ -\infty along Ker ​ Σ ^ \mathrm{Ker}\,\hat{\Sigma} . In this regime, the direction of divergence followed by a given procedure is not determined by L L alone but also depends on the optimization algorithm and its initialization, which is usually referred to as an implicit bias of the optimization algorithm ( Gunasekar et al., 2018 ) . Our goal is to compare the implicit biases of two algorithms. First, we study gradient descent initialized at A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 and write A K A_{K} for the parameter obtained after K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 gradient steps on ( 8 ). We then compare with the iterate A K σ A^{\sigma}_{K} obtained by running K K steps of gradient descent, from the same initialization, on a diffusion-style noised objective. Fix a noise level σ > 0 \sigma>0 and let ω ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ I ) \omega\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\operatorname{I}) . The noised objective is L σ : A ↦ 1 m ​ ∑ i = 1 m 𝔼 ω ​ [ ∇ ⋅ s A ​ ( x i + ω ) + 1 2 ​ ∥ s A ​ ( x i + ω ) ∥ 2 ] . L_{\sigma}:A\mapsto\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\big[\nabla\cdot s_{A}(x_{i}+\omega)+\frac{1}{2}\lVert s_{A}(x_{i}+\omega)\rVert^{2}\big]. As shown by Vincent (2011) , this coincides, up to an A A -independent constant, with the standard denoising score-matching regression objective. Additionally, a direct computation shows that L σ ​ ( A ) = L ⁡ ( A ) + σ 2 2 ​ ∥ A ∥ F 2 . L_{\sigma}(A)=L(A)+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\lVert A\rVert_{F}^{2}. Thus, it is equivalent to adding a ridge-type regularization term. We show that, in this Gaussian setting, noise injection does not fundamentally change the learned score: both procedures recover the empirical covariance Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} on its range, up to a shift of order σ 2 \sigma^{2} , and differ only in how they regularize its kernel. The key takeaway is that the benefit of the noising process identified in the sampling phase has no counterpart in the learning phase, at least in the Gaussian setting considered here. Since A A plays the role of the precision matrix Σ − 1 \Sigma^{-1} in the score model s A ​ ( x ) = − A ​ x s_{A}(x)=-Ax , Theorem 7 below characterizes, up to an exponentially decaying error, the covariance matrices estimated by each procedure—namely A K − 1 A_{K}^{-1} and ( A K σ ) − 1 (A_{K}^{\sigma})^{-1} . Let us denote by λ ^ max \hat{\lambda}_{\max} the largest eigenvalue of Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} , λ ^ min \hat{\lambda}_{\min} its smallest eigenvalue, λ ^ min + \hat{\lambda}_{\min}^{+} its smallest positive eigenvalue and Π Ker ​ Σ ^ \Pi_{\mathrm{Ker}\,\hat{\Sigma}} the orthogonal projector onto its kernel, of dimension max ⁡ ( 0 , d − m ) \max(0,d-m) almost surely. Theorem 7 (Score learning) . Consider gradient descent initialized at A 0 = 0 A_{0}=0 , with step-size α > 0 \alpha>0 , on both L L and L σ L_{\sigma} . Let K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 . • If α < 2 λ ^ max \alpha<\frac{2}{\hat{\lambda}_{\max}} , the iterate A K A_{K} is invertible and A K − 1 = Σ ^ + 1 K ​ α ​ Π Ker ​ Σ ^ + O ⁡ ( ρ 1 K ) , A_{K}^{-1}=\hat{\Sigma}+\frac{1}{K\alpha}\Pi_{\mathrm{Ker}\,\hat{\Sigma}}+O(\rho_{1}^{K}), with ρ 1 = max ⁡ ( | 1 − α ​ λ ^ min + | , | 1 − α ​ λ ^ max | ) < 1 . \rho_{1}=\max\big(\lvert 1-\alpha\hat{\lambda}_{\min}^{+}\rvert,\lvert 1-\alpha\hat{\lambda}_{\max}\rvert\big)<1. • If α < 2 λ ^ max + σ 2 \alpha<\frac{2}{\hat{\lambda}_{\max}+\sigma^{2}} , the iterate A K σ A_{K}^{\sigma} is invertible and ( A K σ ) − 1 = Σ ^ + σ 2 ​ I + O ⁡ ( ρ 2 K ) , (A_{K}^{\sigma})^{-1}=\hat{\Sigma}+\sigma^{2}\operatorname{I}+O(\rho_{2}^{K}), with ρ 2 = max ⁡ ( | 1 − α ⁡ ( λ ^ min + σ 2 ) | , | 1 − α ⁡ ( λ ^ max + σ 2 ) | ) < 1 . \rho_{2}=\max\big(\lvert 1-\alpha(\hat{\lambda}_{\min}+\sigma^{2})\rvert,\lvert 1-\alpha(\hat{\lambda}_{\max}+\sigma^{2})\rvert\big)<1. The distinction between the two procedures is clearest when Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} is singular, that is, almost surely when m < d m<d . For the standard score-matching loss L L , the resulting non-identifiability is resolved implicitly by gradient descent: up to an exponentially small optimization error, A K − 1 A_{K}^{-1} coincides with Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} on its range, while a correction of order 1 / ( K ​ α ) 1/(K\alpha) appears only in the kernel of Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} . In contrast, the noised objective L σ L_{\sigma} induces an explicit ridge regularization, and this translates into a uniform covariance shift σ 2 ​ I \sigma^{2}\operatorname{I} : all directions are regularized by the same amount. Thus the two procedures recover a regularized empirical covariance matrix, but differ slightly in the regularization: the implicit bias of L L acts only in directions that are not identified by the data, whereas noise injection regularizes all directions indiscriminately. Yet, in order to recover the true covariance directions, one should take σ 2 ≪ λ ^ min + \sigma^{2}\ll\hat{\lambda}_{\min}^{+} and, respectively, 1 / ( K ​ α ) ≪ λ ^ min + 1/(K\alpha)\ll\hat{\lambda}_{\min}^{+} . In this regime, both regularizations are essentially identical, meaning that the noising process does not help regularize the estimated score compared to learning the original score (with early stopping). We finally note that this constitutes an instance where the gradient descent path follows the explicit ridge regularization path, which is a structure appearing in many contexts ( Ali et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: This work demonstrates an advantage of modeling the score at various levels of noise in the Gaussian setting: more efficient sampling by gradually adding anisotropy. This benefit is specific to sampling: in the same setting, the score learned with noise coincides, up to the regularization of the empirical nullspace, with the one learned without. Our sampling results take the form of scaling laws, both for the sampling error and for the hyperparameters that achieve it. We emphasize that, despite its simplicity, the Gaussian framework enables a rigorous proof by characterizing the exact dependence on the condition number. Weaker assumptions, e.g. , log-concavity, lead to loose dependence on the condition number, which is insufficient for our purpose. Natural directions for future work include incorporating the score estimation error into the sampling analysis and extending the comparison beyond the Gaussian setting.

sections.heading: B.1 Overview
sections.text: This section is devoted to the proof of the following theorem, stated in Section 2.2 . See 1

sections.heading: Error decomposition.
sections.text: ULA and ULD define time-homogeneous Markov chains. Under stability conditions on the hyperparameters, established in step (i) below, these chains converge, not to the target ℙ \mathbb{P} , but to an invariant law ℙ ∞ \mathbb{P}_{\infty} that depends on the step-size η \eta (and on the friction γ \gamma for ULD). The triangle inequality W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ∞ ) + W 2 ​ ( ℙ ∞ , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}_{\infty})+W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{\infty},\mathbb{P}) (10) separates two contributions. The first term is the early-stopping error: after N N iterations, the chain has not yet reached its invariant law. The second is the discretization error: the bias of ℙ ∞ \mathbb{P}_{\infty} with respect to ℙ \mathbb{P} , introduced by the Euler–Maruyama scheme.

sections.heading: Reduction to eigenvalues.
sections.text: Lemma A.1 applies to both algorithms (Remark A.2 ): each ℙ N \mathbb{P}_{N} is a centered Gaussian whose covariance Σ N \Sigma_{N} lies in 𝒜 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathcal{A}(\Sigma) , and so does the covariance Σ ∞ \Sigma_{\infty} of ℙ ∞ \mathbb{P}_{\infty} , the limit of ( Σ N ) (\Sigma_{N}) . By Lemma A.3 , both terms in ( 10 ) then depend only on the eigenvalues λ i ( N ) \lambda_{i}^{(N)} of Σ N \Sigma_{N} , λ i ∞ \lambda_{i}^{\infty} of Σ ∞ \Sigma_{\infty} and λ i \lambda_{i} of Σ \Sigma : W 2 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ∞ ) = ∑ i = 1 d ( λ i ( N ) − λ i ∞ ) 2 , W 2 2 ​ ( ℙ ∞ , ℙ ) = ∑ i = 1 d ( λ i ∞ − λ i ) 2 . W_{2}^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}_{\infty})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{i}^{(N)}}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}^{\infty}}\Big)^{2},\quad W_{2}^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{\infty},\mathbb{P})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{i}^{\infty}}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\Big)^{2}. (11) This is the payoff of the Gaussian setting: the analysis reduces to real sequences for which closed forms are available. Throughout, a choice of hyperparameters is called admissible if it lies in the stability range of the chain, shrunk by numerical constants that give the estimates some slack, keeping the denominators involved bounded away from zero. Remarks B.4 and B.11 make the gap with the exact stability conditions explicit.

sections.heading: Outline.
sections.text: Sections B.2 (ULA) and B.3 (ULD) follow the same four steps. (i) Closed form. Compute the eigenvalues λ i ( N ) \lambda_{i}^{(N)} and λ i ∞ \lambda_{i}^{\infty} from the scalar recursions of Lemma A.1 , and identify the stability conditions under which ( Σ N ) (\Sigma_{N}) converges. (ii) Parametric bound. Bound each of the two terms in ( 10 ) and sum: this gives a bound on W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) valid over the whole admissible range identified in (i) (Proposition B.1 for ULA, Proposition B.7 for ULD). (iii) Choice of hyperparameters. Minimize, up to a numerical constant, the bound obtained in (ii), and check that the selected values satisfy the stability conditions as soon as N ≥ N ⋆ N\geq N_{\star} . (iv) Asymptotic equivalent. For the hyperparameters of step (iii), derive an exact equivalent of W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) as N → ∞ N\to\infty from the closed forms of step (i). This equivalent has the same order log ⁡ N / N \log N/N and the same spectral prefactor as the bound of step (iii), up to a numerical constant: the bound is of the right order of magnitude.

sections.heading: B.2 Unadjusted Langevin algorithm
sections.text: The goal of this section is to prove the following proposition, which bounds W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) for every small enough step-size η \eta . To lighten notation, we drop the index i i whenever we argue at a fixed eigendirection i i . Proposition B.1 (Parametric bound for ULA) . For any step-size 0 < η ≤ λ min 0<\eta\leq\lambda_{\min} and any N ≥ 0 N\geq 0 , the error of ULA satisfies W 2 ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ 2 ​ Tr ⁡ Σ e − 2 η N / λ max + 1 2 Tr ⁡ ( Σ − 1 ) η . W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq\sqrt{2\Tr\Sigma}\,e^{-2\eta N/\lambda_{\max}}+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\Tr(\Sigma^{-1})}\,\eta. The two terms of this bound come from bounding the early-stopping error and the discretization error respectively. The first decays exponentially in N ​ η N\eta , the time at which the process is stopped, while the second grows linearly with the step-size η \eta . The step-size selected in Theorem 1 is the best compromise between these two competing effects.

sections.heading: B.3 Underdamped Langevin dynamics
sections.text: The proof of Theorem 1 for ULD follows the structure of the previous section. We first prove the proposition below, which bounds W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) for all ( η , γ ) (\eta,\gamma) satisfying one of two sets of assumptions: a large-friction regime, which is the one adopted in Theorem 1 , and a small-friction regime. Both lead to similar bounds, up to numerical constants; Remark B.8 explains why the first one is retained in Theorem 1 . Proposition B.7 (Parametric bound for ULD) . Let N ≥ 0 N\geq 0 . In the large-friction regime γ ≥ 8 / λ min and η ≤ 1 γ , \gamma\geq\sqrt{8/\lambda_{\min}}\quad\text{and}\quad\eta\leq\frac{1}{\gamma}, (LF) the error of ULD satisfies W 2 ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ 8 Tr ⁡ Σ e − 2 η N / ( λ max γ ) + 6 7 Tr ⁡ ( Σ − 1 ) η γ , W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq 8\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma}\,e^{-2\eta N/(\lambda_{\max}\gamma)}+\frac{6}{7}\sqrt{\Tr(\Sigma^{-1})}\,\frac{\eta}{\gamma}, and in the small-friction regime γ ≤ 2 / λ max and η ≤ 1 2 ​ λ min ​ γ , \gamma\leq\sqrt{2/\lambda_{\max}}\quad\text{and}\quad\eta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{\min}\gamma, (SF) it satisfies W 2 ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ 8 Tr ⁡ Σ e − η γ N / 2 + 3 2 Tr ⁡ ( Σ − 1 ) η γ . W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq 8\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma}\,e^{-\eta\gamma N/2}+\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{\Tr(\Sigma^{-1})}\,\frac{\eta}{\gamma}. Here too, each bound is the sum of an early-stopping term and a discretization term. Up to a numerical constant, the discretization term has the same expression in both regimes. Only the early-stopping term changes, with the friction γ \gamma appearing in the denominator or in the numerator of the exponent according to whether it is large or small. Remark B.8 . The small-friction bound of Proposition B.7 is strictly decreasing in γ \gamma . There is no trade-off: one simply saturates the constraint γ ≤ 2 / λ max \gamma\leq\sqrt{2/\lambda_{\max}} , which also makes the admissible range η ≤ 1 2 ​ λ min ​ γ \eta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{\min}\gamma as wide as possible. The resulting rates are the same in both regimes. We retain the large-friction regime ( LF ) in Theorem 1 because the roots r ± r_{\pm} introduced below are then real and positive, which keeps the analysis simplest, and because the bound has exactly the form of the ULA bound with ϕ := η / γ \phi:=\eta/\gamma in place of η \eta ; with the hyperparameters of the theorem, ϕ = 1 2 ​ λ max ​ log ⁡ N N \phi=\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{\max}\frac{\log N}{N} is precisely the ULA step-size.

sections.heading: C.1 Overview
sections.text: We now turn to the proof of the following theorem, stated in Section 2.3 . See 3 Proposition 4 , which differs from Theorem 3 only through the choice of hyperparameters, is restated and proved in Section C.3 .

sections.heading: Error decomposition.
sections.text: The error of the diffusion algorithm of Section 2.1 combines three sources. The first is the initialization error: the process is started from Y 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , T ​ I ) Y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,T\operatorname{I}) as a proxy for the true marginal ℚ T = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Σ + T ​ I ) \mathbb{Q}_{T}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma+T\operatorname{I}) , which is unknown a priori . It is measured by the Wasserstein distance W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ~ N ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N}) between the law ℙ N \mathbb{P}_{N} actually sampled and the law ℙ ~ N \tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N} that would have been sampled from the exact initialization Y 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Σ + T ​ I ) Y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma+T\operatorname{I}) . The second is the discretization error incurred when simulating the reverse SDE ( 5 ): it is W 2 ​ ( ℙ ~ N , ℚ δ ) W_{2}(\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N},\mathbb{Q}_{\delta}) , the distance, for an exact initialization, between the law produced by the discrete scheme and the law ℚ δ = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , Σ + δ ​ I ) \mathbb{Q}_{\delta}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma+\delta\operatorname{I}) reached by the continuous process. The third is the early-stopping error W 2 ​ ( ℚ δ , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{\delta},\mathbb{P}) , due to stopping the continuous process at the threshold δ > 0 \delta>0 . The triangle inequality formalizes this decomposition: W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ~ N ) + W 2 ​ ( ℙ ~ N , ℚ δ ) + W 2 ​ ( ℚ δ , ℙ ) . W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N})+W_{2}(\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N},\mathbb{Q}_{\delta})+W_{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{\delta},\mathbb{P}). (60)

sections.text: All the laws in ( 60 ) are centered Gaussians with covariance in 𝒜 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathcal{A}(\Sigma) : this is immediate for ℙ \mathbb{P} and ℚ δ \mathbb{Q}_{\delta} , and follows from Lemma A.1 for ℙ N \mathbb{P}_{N} and ℙ ~ N \tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N} . Lemma A.3 therefore applies and, denoting by λ i ( N ) \lambda_{i}^{(N)} and λ ~ i ( N ) \tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(N)} the eigenvalues of the covariances of ℙ N \mathbb{P}_{N} and ℙ ~ N \tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N} , we record for later use W 2 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ~ N ) \displaystyle W_{2}^{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N}) = ∑ i = 1 d ( λ i ( N ) − λ ~ i ( N ) ) 2 , \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{i}^{(N)}}-\sqrt{\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(N)}}\Big)^{2}, (61) W 2 2 ​ ( ℙ ~ N , ℚ δ ) \displaystyle W_{2}^{2}(\tilde{\mathbb{P}}_{N},\mathbb{Q}_{\delta}) = ∑ i = 1 d ( λ ~ i ( N ) − λ i + δ ) 2 , \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sqrt{\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(N)}}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}+\delta}\Big)^{2}, (62) W 2 2 ​ ( ℚ δ , ℙ ) \displaystyle W_{2}^{2}(\mathbb{Q}_{\delta},\mathbb{P}) = ∑ i = 1 d ( λ i + δ − λ i ) 2 . \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{i}+\delta}-\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}\Big)^{2}. (63)

sections.heading: Outline.
sections.text: The proof of Theorem 3 follows the same steps as that of Theorem 1 . (i)–(ii) Parametric bound (Section C.2 ). Closed form of the eigenvalues λ i ( N ) \lambda_{i}^{(N)} and λ ~ i ( N ) \tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(N)} from the scalar recursions of Lemma A.1 , then separate bounds on the three terms of ( 60 ), and summation. This gives a bound on W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) in which T T and δ \delta remain free (Proposition C.1 ). (iii) Choice of hyperparameters (Section C.3 ). Plug the hyperparameters of Theorem 3 and Proposition 4 into the bound of Proposition C.1 . (iv) Asymptotic equivalent (Section C.4 ). Exact equivalent of W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) as N → ∞ N\to\infty for any geometric grid with T ∝ N T\propto\sqrt{N} and δ ∝ N − 2 \delta\propto N^{-2} , from the closed forms of step (i). This equivalent does not depend on the proportionality constants, which shows that the spectral rate is a robust feature of the scheme.

sections.heading: C.2 Parametric bound for the diffusion sampler
sections.text: The goal of this section is to prove the following proposition, which bounds W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P}) for all values of the hyperparameters. As before, we freely drop the eigenvalue index i i in the proofs. Proposition C.1 (Parametric bound for the diffusion sampler) . For every N ≥ 1 N\geq 1 and every T > δ > 0 T>\delta>0 , with the geometric discretization τ k = T ​ ( δ / T ) k / N \tau_{k}=T(\delta/T)^{k/N} , the error of the diffusion algorithm satisfies W 2 ​ ( ℙ N , ℙ ) ≤ Tr ⁡ ( ( Σ + δ ​ I ) 3 ​ Σ 2 ) T 2 + Tr ⁡ Σ + 4 ​ d ​ δ 4 ​ N ​ ( T δ ) 1 / N ​ log ⁡ T δ + d ​ δ . W_{2}(\mathbb{P}_{N},\mathbb{P})\leq\frac{\sqrt{\Tr((\Sigma+\delta\operatorname{I})^{3}\Sigma^{2})}}{T^{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{\Tr\Sigma+4d\delta}}{4N}\Big(\frac{T}{\delta}\Big)^{1/N}\log\frac{T}{\delta}+\sqrt{d\delta}. The three terms bound the initialization, discretization and early-stopping errors respectively.

text: Diffusion Removes Langevin’s Conditioning Dependence: A Sharp Gaussian Analysis Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.12052v1 [stat.ML] 08 Oct 2026 Diffusion Removes Langevin’s Conditioning Dependence: A Sharp Gaussian Analysis Adam Perbost Francis Bach Pierre Marion Affiliation: Inria, École normale supérieure – PSL Research University Affiliation: Paris, France Email: ${$adam.perbost,francis.bach,pierre.marion$}$@inria.fr Abstract Despite their empirical success, why diffusion models overcome the bottlenecks of classical score-based samplers remains unclear. In this work, we leverage Gaussian distributions to isolate this phenomenon. We establish 2-Wasserstein convergence bounds for optimized hyperparameters, showing that diffusion processes achieve a sampling error of O ⁡ ( d ​ λ max ​ log ⁡ N / N ) O(\sqrt{d\lambda_{\max}}\log N/N) , where d d is the dimension, N N the number of sampling steps, and λ max \lambda_{\max} the largest eigenvalue of the target covariance matrix. Unadjusted and underdamped Langevin dynamics suffer from an additional κ \sqrt{\kappa} factor, where κ \kappa is the condition number. These rates follow from spectral bounds which are sharp: we confirm them via matching first-order asymptotics as N → ∞ N\rightarrow\infty . Our analysis provides a rigorous characterization, in the Gaussian setting, of how time-dependent score trajectories remove condition-number dependence during sampling. By contrast, in the learning phase, we show that estimating the unnoised score by gradient descent leads to essentially the same estimator as estimating a noisy score, which suggests that the benefits of noising do not come from the learning phase. 1 Introduction Since their introduction, diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) have achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of domains ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Kong et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . Training diffusion models requires estimating the gradient of the log-density (the so-called score ) of a noisy version of the target. Then samples are produced by iterative denoising through a formula involving this score. Taking a step back, iterative score-based sampling strategies long predate modern diffusion models, as epitomized by the celebrated Langevin algorithm ( Pavliotis, 2014 ; Roberts and Tweedie, 1996 ) and its many variants such as underdamped Langevin ( Leimkuhler and Matthews, 2015 ) . The key factors explaining their success compared to those more classical algorithms are still unclear: what exact role does the noising process in diffusion models play, and how does it interact with the learning and sampling phases? Our primary goal in this work is to prove a separation in sampling efficiency between diffusion models and Langevin dynamics in terms of their dependence on the condition number. This sheds light on the practical effectiveness of diffusion models on ill-conditioned distributions such as natural images ( Guth et al., 2022 ; Field, 1987 ) . To do so, we consider the class of (centered) Gaussian targets. Naturally, sampling from a Gaussian distribution is not our primary concern here. Rather, we use this analytically tractable setting to derive sharp convergence rates accompanied by matching asymptotics, in order to highlight how diffusion models overcome limitations of other score-based sampling methods. As discussed below, deriving tight condition-number dependence for more general target classes such as log-concave distributions is a long-standing open problem ( Cheng et al., 2018 ; Dalalyan and Riou-Durand, 2020 ) , which is outside the scope of the present paper. Additionally, we focus for most of the paper on the sampling phase, comparing the sampling convergence rates of diffusion, unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and underdamped Langevin dynamics (ULD). Assuming access to the true score yields a clean analysis and the separation between diffusion and Langevin, hence for simplicity we focus on this case. The connection with the estimation of the score in the learning phase is discussed in the latter part of our work. Contributions. We establish upper bounds on the 2-Wasserstein error between the target distribution and the distribution sampled from the diffusion, ULA and ULD. Convergence rates are derived in Section 2 by optimizing these bounds with respect to hyperparameters (see Table 1 for summary). The bounds for diffusion and for Langevin differ by a factor proportional to the square root of the condition number. Thanks to explicit computations of the Wasserstein errors, we confirm these rates via matching first-order asymptotics. By contrast, in the learning phase, we show in Section 3 that estimating the unnoised score by gradient descent leads to essentially the same estimator as estimating a noisy score, the two differing only in how they regularize the directions unseen in the data, which suggests that the benefits of noising do not come from the learning phase. For ULA, a similar analysis of the two error terms was already performed, for example, by Durmus et al. (2019) ; Wibisono (2018) and specifically in the Gaussian case by Pedregosa (2023) . Building upon these works, we perform hyperparameter optimization and compute the asymptotic equivalent (rather than upper bounds). Many works have studied ULD in the log-concave case, see, e.g. , Cheng et al. (2018) ; Dalalyan and Riou-Durand (2020) ; Leimkuhler et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2026) for studies of the stochastic Euler scheme and Euler–Maruyama (EM) integrators. This line of work yields loose dependence on the condition number due to the bias term induced by non-vanishing step-sizes (see, e.g. , Eq. (11) in Dalalyan and Riou-Durand (2020) with a κ 3 / 2 \kappa^{3/2} in the complexity bound compared to our κ \sqrt{\kappa} ). A line of work has proved improved condition dependence for Gaussian targets ( Shen and Lee, 2019 ; Apers et al., 2024 ; Gouraud et al., 2025 ) , albeit with more complex integrators (splitting, random step-sizes, or Metropolis corrections). To our knowledge, the tight study of the bias of ULD for a Gaussian target and the EM integrator is a novel contribution. For diffusion models, Pierret and Galerne (2025) derive and numerically analyze error terms for Gaussian targets, but do not analytically derive optimal hyperparameters, discuss the dependence on the condition number, nor derive asymptotic equivalents. Closer are the works by Hurault et al. (2025) and Hurault et al. (2026) , which derive Wasserstein bounds for Gaussian data and discuss optimal hyperparameter choices depending on the covariance spectrum. A key difference with our work is that their analysis holds asymptotically for small step-sizes, whereas we make a fully non-asymptotic analysis (albeit in less generality), which enables us to capture the interaction between the step-size and other parameters, and to derive optimal step complexity with respect to our bounds. Wasserstein bounds beyond the Gaussian case are given for instance by Strasman et al.
